indicators.title: Executable disguised with a document-style double extension
indicators.rationale: The filename 'Q3_Vendor_Invoice.pdf.exe' ends in a document extension followed by an executable extension. Windows hides known extensions by default, so users may see only the document-like part. This is a common social-engineering technique; legitimate software rarely uses it.

indicators.title: Section is both writable and executable
indicators.rationale: Sections marked WRITE+EXECUTE allow code to be modified at run time, which packers and self-modifying loaders rely on. Some legitimate JIT-based or older software also does this.

indicators.title: High-entropy section
indicators.rationale: Entropy at or above 7.2 bits/byte indicates compressed or encrypted content, which can hide code from static analysis. Legitimate installers, compressed resources and media also score this high, so this indicator alone is weak.

indicators.title: Imports consistent with process injection
indicators.rationale: The import table combines APIs that write into and start execution inside another process. Debuggers, security products and some management tools legitimately use the same APIs.

indicators.title: HTTP client APIs together with embedded URLs
indicators.rationale: The binary imports HTTP client functionality and contains hard-coded URLs, so it is able to contact the listed destinations. Whether it does so, and why, cannot be established statically.

indicators.title: Persistence capability (service/registry APIs with autostart references)
indicators.rationale: Service-installation or registry-write APIs are imported and the strings reference autostart locations or scheduled-task tooling. Installers legitimately do this; context is required.

indicators.title: Debugger detection API imported
indicators.rationale: Debugger checks are inserted by many compilers' runtime libraries; noted for context only.

indicators.title: Non-standard section names
indicators.rationale: Section names outside the usual compiler set can indicate custom tooling or packing; they can also be produced by less common compilers.

indicators.title: Data appended after the last section (overlay)
indicators.rationale: Overlays are used by installers and signed binaries (certificate tables) but also to carry encrypted payloads or configuration. Overlay size 2056 bytes, entropy 7.915.

indicators.title: Compile timestamp recorded
indicators.rationale: The PE timestamp is trivially forgeable; it is recorded for context and is not used for timeline reconstruction.

indicators.title: Embedded hidden/encoded PowerShell command line
indicators.rationale: A string builds a PowerShell command line with hidden window and/or encoded command options. Encoded commands obscure what is executed and are frequently abused; some administrative tools also use them.

indicators.title: Network indicators embedded in strings
indicators.rationale: Hard-coded URLs and IP addresses are extracted as potential IOCs. Their presence does not show they were contacted; correlate with network evidence.

content.analyst_conclusions:
[Demonstration analyst notes for the SIMULATED Meridian case]

Confirmed (directly supported by evidence):
- Q3_Vendor_Invoice.pdf.exe was downloaded through the webmail session on WS-FIN-042 and its SHA-256 matches the acquired sample and the EDR file-creation record.
- The same image was executed by jmorales; its process lineage (PID/parent PID) includes PowerShell, msync.exe, a scheduled task, a service and a new local administrator account.
- Files in Documents\Confidential were read by processes in that lineage, an archive was created, and 48 MB were sent to 203.0.113.77:443.
- The 'Windows PowerShell' event log was cleared by jmorales' session.

Hypotheses (require validation):
- The outbound transfer contained the archived confidential documents (content not captured; supported by timing, archive size and script block text).
- The failed logons from WS-HR-015 at 12:58 UTC are unrelated (no shared entity with the sequence).

Recommended next steps: isolate WS-FIN-042, acquire memory and full disk image, review proxy content logs for upload.meridian-sync.example, reset jmorales credentials and remove svc_msync.

standard: All findings are derived from the acquired artifacts only. Activity that was not logged (audit policy not enabled, logs rotated or cleared) is invisible to this analysis; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
Static malware analysis does not execute samples. Packed, encrypted or staged payloads and run-time behaviour cannot be fully characterised statically.
YARA matches confirm that bytes satisfy a rule's condition; the significance of a match depends on the rule and is explained per match.
Correlations are hypotheses built from timestamps and shared entities (file names, hashes, process IDs, embedded indicators). They indicate plausible sequences and do not prove causation.
Timestamps from different sources are normalised to UTC. Clock skew between systems and timezone assumptions for sources without timezone information can affect ordering.
Process IDs are reused by Windows; PID-based lineage is bounded by host and correlation window but could mis-link processes in long investigations.
Indicator assessments ('watchlist match', 'suspicious') reflect local reference data and findings, not external threat intelligence. No commercial or online reputation service was queried.

The audit ledger is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof: an actor with write access to the database could rewrite the entire chain. Compare the ledger head hash with an independently stored copy to detect that.
TraceForge does not certify legal admissibility or compliance with any specific chain-of-custody standard.
